podcast.title: Kurt Cobain's Death Impact (1994)
podcast.body: The death of Kurt Cobain in April 1994 temporarily shocked Lane Staley into sobriety. "Kurt Cobain's death in April 1994 scared him sober for a bit, but addiction came calling again."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Demri Parrott's Influence and Death (1996)
podcast.body: Lane Staley's former fiancée, Demri Parrott, was also addicted to drugs, and it appeared her use began after meeting him. She made repeated attempts to get clean, and after each release from hospitalization, she would spend weeks trying to help Lane, but neither of them succeeded. Her death from a drug overdose on October 29, 1996, deeply affected Staley, even though they had broken up earlier, leading to him being placed on a 24-hour suicide watch, and he reportedly never recovered from her passing. "It didn't help that his former fiance, Demory Parade, was also a junkie, and when she died of a drug overdose on October 29, 1996, Lane fell apart, even though they'd broken up sometime earlier."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Band Breakup and Sean Kinney's Efforts (November 1997 - 2002)
podcast.body: Alice in Chains officially broke up in November 1997 due to Layne Staley's inactivity as their frontman. Despite the breakup, drummer Sean Kinney regularly checked in on Staley, visiting his condo at least three times a week to ensure he was "okay," or as okay as circumstances allowed. Staley, however, was highly withdrawn, often ignoring calls and visitors at his door. "With nothing happening with their frontman, Allison Chains broke up in November 1997. Over the years that followed Lane deteriorated."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Condo Purchase (1997)
podcast.body: In April 1997, Layne Staley moved into a three-bedroom, 1500 square foot condo in Seattle's University District, purchased for $262,000. The property was bought by the LaRusta Trust, which was part of the Alice in Chains Management Company, using "John LaRusta" as an alias to avoid his real name appearing on public records. "The purchaser was the LaRusta Trust, which was part of the Allison Chains Management Company. John LaRusta was an alias used by Lane."

podcast.title: Condo Purchase and Isolation (April 1997)
podcast.body: In April 1997, Layne Staley moved into a three-bedroom, 1500 square foot condo in Seattle's University District, purchased for $262,000 by the LaRusta Trust, part of the Alice in Chains Management Company. Staley used "John LaRusta" as an alias to keep his real name out of public records. He spent his time painting, watching TV, playing video games, and doing "lots and lots of drugs." Alice in Chains guitarist Jerry Cantrell installed a home recording outfit for him, which Staley used only occasionally, further highlighting his increasing isolation. "The purchaser was the LaRusta Trust, which was part of the Allison Chains Management Company. John LaRusta was an alias used by Lane. He did one his real name used in any public records."

podcast.title: Five Years of Decline (1997-2002)
podcast.body: Following Demri Parrott's death, Lane Staley spent five years in a severe decline, marked by intensified drug use and deteriorating health, leading to his eventual death. "And Lane spent the next five years, from 1997 to 2002, dying."

podcast.body: After Alice in Chains broke up in November 1997 due to Layne Staley's inactivity, guitarist Jerry Cantrell installed a home recording outfit in Layne's condo. However, Layne rarely used it, spending most of his time painting, watching TV, playing video games, and consuming "lots and lots of drugs." "With nothing happening with their frontman, Allison Chains broke up in November 1997."

podcast.title: Physical Manifestations of Illness (1998)
podcast.body: By 1998, there were rumors that Lane Staley had contracted gangrene from continuous needle use and had stopped eating due to rotting teeth, only being able to consume protein drinks designed for seniors. "By 1998, there were more rumors that he had contracted gang green from nonstop needle use, that he'd stopped eating because his teeth were rotting out."

podcast.title: Cause and Date of Death (2002)
podcast.body: The medical examiner determined Layne Staley had been dead since approximately April 5th, which coincided with the anniversary of Kurt Cobain's suicide. The official cause of death was an overdose of a mix of heroin and cocaine, but his body was in such a terrible state that it was considered "just a matter of time." "The medical examiner later said that he'd been there since about April 5, the anniversary of when we think Kurt Cobain killed himself. The official cause of death was an overdose of a mix of heroin and cocaine, but it was just a matter of time because his body was in such terrible, terrible shape."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Death (April 5, 2002)
podcast.body: Layne Staley died on or about April 5, 2002, a date notably eight years after Kurt Cobain's death. His death was discovered on April 19, 2002, after his accountants noticed no bank withdrawals for weeks. Seattle police found him on his couch with a heroin cooker and syringe nearby after forcing entry into his dead-bolted condo. "The best guess the corner could come up with is that Lane died on or about April 5. The same day on which Kurt Cobain had died eight years earlier."

podcast.title: Death by Overdose (April 5, 2002)
podcast.body: Layne Staley's body was found on April 19, 2002, approximately two weeks after his death, which the medical examiner estimated occurred around April 5, 2002 – the anniversary of Kurt Cobain's death. The official cause of death was an overdose of a mix of heroin and cocaine. He weighed only 86 pounds at the time of discovery, with a syringe sticking out of his leg and another fully loaded syringe in his hand. The condo was littered with drugs, crackpipes, and a stash of coke. His death was not a surprise, as he had been a "drugged up mess" for years, with a Seattle music paper reportedly having an obituary ready for him in the mid-90s. "The official cause of death was an overdose of a mix of heroin and cocaine, but it was just a matter of time because his body was in such terrible, terrible shape."

On April 19th, Layne's mother and Seattle police broke down the door to his condo. He was found dead on the couch, weighing only 86 pounds, with a syringe sticking out of his leg and another loaded syringe in his hand. The apartment was littered with drugs, crackpipes, and a stash of cocaine. "On April 19, Lane's mom went to the condo with Seattle police. They broke down the door and found Lane, who weighed just 86 pounds. He was dead on the couch."

podcast.title: Discovery of Death (April 19, 2002)
podcast.body: Layne Staley's death was discovered on April 19, 2002, by Seattle police after his accountants alerted his mother and stepfather that there had been no withdrawals from his bank accounts for weeks. Police found him on his couch with drug paraphernalia. "Just after 5.30 in the afternoon of April 19, 2002, Seattle police kicked in the dead-bolted door of Lane's condo."

podcast.title: Final Days and Discovery (April 2002)
podcast.body: In his final years, Layne Staley lived as a recluse, rarely leaving his condo except for occasional visits to a local bar called The Rainbow, where he would sit in a back corner, drink, and pass out. His extreme withdrawal meant that his death went unnoticed for approximately two weeks. Accountants managing his financial affairs noticed his bank account hadn't been touched, prompting concern. On April 19, his mother, accompanied by Seattle Police, broke down his door and found him dead on the couch. "He was so withdrawn and so much of a hermit that it wasn't until the accountants in charge of Lane's financial affairs noticed that his bank account had been touched for two weeks that they suspected that something might be wrong."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Final Visit from Mike Starr (April 4, 2002)
podcast.body: On Thursday, April 4, 2002, former bandmate Mike Starr visited Lane Staley's condo and was shocked by his emaciated appearance, offering to call 911. Staley vehemently refused, stating he would never speak to Starr again if he did. Starr left feeling angry and discouraged, with Staley pleading, "not like this, don't leave like this." Mike Starr is believed to have been the last person to see Lane Staley alive. "Mike was shocked at how bad Lane looked, an offer to call 911. Lane said, if you do that, I will never talk to you again."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Friends' Efforts and Isolation (2002)
podcast.body: In early 2002, despite attempts to record with Layne Staley, his singing voice was gone, and he had developed a lisp due to his missing teeth. Alice in Chains drummer Sean Kinney regularly checked Layne's condo online three times a week to ensure he was okay. Layne became extremely withdrawn, often ignoring calls and visitors at his door. His occasional outings consisted mainly of going to a local bar called The Rainbow, where he would sit in a back corner, drink, and pass out. "Allison Chains drummer Sean Kinney made sure that he checked in online at his condo at least three times a week just to make sure that everything was okay, or as okay as circumstances allowed."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Long-term Deterioration (Late 1990s - 2002)
podcast.body: Layne Staley's death came as no surprise, as he had been a "drugged out mess for years," largely unable to care for himself. The Seattle music paper, The Rocket, reportedly had an obituary prepared for him since the mid-1990s. His health steadily deteriorated, leaving him looking like an "emaciated 80-year-old man" with no teeth and atrophied legs that made walking and standing difficult. "When he passed, it really was no surprise. Lane had been a drugged out mess for years, unable to do much of anything for himself."

podcast.title: Mike Starr's Death (2011)
podcast.body: Mike Starr, the last person believed to have seen Lane Staley alive, also died prematurely from a prescription drug overdose on March 8, 2011, having been addicted himself. "Mike Star, the last guy to see Lane alive, died himself of a prescription drug overdose on March 8, 2011."

podcast.title: Autopsy and Cause of Death
podcast.body: The autopsy determined Lane Staley had been dead for two weeks, likely dying on Friday, April 5, 2002—the day after Mike Starr's visit and coincidentally the same day Kurt Cobain died in 1994. The cause of death was ruled an accidental overdose of a speedball, a mixture of cocaine and heroin. His body was severely decomposed, weighing only 39 kilograms (80 pounds), and dental records were required for identification, which was challenging due to the loss of most of his teeth. He was 34 years old. "Pause of death was ruled as an accidental overdose of a speedball, a mix of coke and heroin."

He became a "hardcore, hermit junkie," having a network of dealers deliver a mix of smack, cocaine, and crack to his condo. "By the late 90s, Lane was in such rough shape that he couldn't tour."

podcast.title: Deteriorating Health and Isolation
podcast.body: During his final years, Lane Staley's health worsened significantly; he suffered from unhealing open sores, and rumors circulated about him losing fingers or an arm due to abscesses. He became increasingly isolated from Alice in Chains and by 1999, rarely left his condo in Seattle's University District, where he primarily painted, played video games, watched TV, and used drugs delivered by dealers, only leaving to withdraw money from a bank machine for payments. "His drug use got much, much heavier. He did start seeing, or at least hanging out with, a woman named Michelle Crane. She spent as much time as she could with him, but his health kept getting worse."

podcast.title: Failed Rehab Attempts
podcast.body: Staley made numerous attempts at rehabilitation, including multiple trips to clinics and having band members fly to be with him in Los Angeles, but none of these efforts proved successful in overcoming his addiction. "There were several trips to rehab clinics, but nothing managed to stick, even when he was sent to LA and had members of the band fly down to be with him."

podcast.title: Family's Unsuccessful Attempts to Help
podcast.body: Despite his mother and other family members attempting to maintain contact and encourage rehab, Lane Staley withdrew further, refusing to answer calls or the door, believing that since 13 previous rehab attempts had failed, further efforts would be futile. "If anyone did reach him and suggested more rehab, he refused. It had already been 13 times, and nothing worked, so why bother?"

podcast.title: Hermit-like Existence
podcast.body: Layne Staley eventually descended into a "hermit light existence" within a "heavily fortified condo in Seattle." His royalty money was deposited directly into a bank account, and his groceries and drugs were delivered to his door. "After a while, Lane descended into a hermit light existence in a heavily fortified condo in Seattle."

podcast.body: Layne Staley, singer for Alice in Chains, was the band's "heaviest user" of drugs, particularly heroin. His drug use intensified with the band's success, leading to countless failed attempts at sobriety in the mid-1990s and increasing isolation, especially after his girlfriend, Demri, died from drug-related complications. podcast.body: By the mid-1990s, Layne Staley's health had deteriorated significantly due to extensive drug use, to the point where "The Rocket," a Seattle music paper, reportedly had an obituary for him ready to go. This indicates that his demise was widely anticipated due to his long-standing and severe struggles with addiction. "The rocket, the Seattle music paper, reportedly had a Lane Staley obituary ready to go, and sometime in the middle of the 90s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Mother's Reflections on His Death
podcast.body: In 2010, Lane Staley's mother appeared on the TV show "Celebrity Rehab," recounting the day his body was found and expressing her sorrow, stating that despite his intelligence, financial resources, time, and 13 prior treatments (including three emergency room visits where he "died three times"), his addiction ultimately claimed his life. "And I told him, I'm so sorry to turn down like this, because I always believed because he was smart. He had the money, and he had the time, and he knew he'd been in treatment 13 times. He'd been in the emergency three times. He died three times. I knew he had what it took. And still it took him out."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Physical Deterioration (Years Leading to Death)
podcast.body: In his final years, Layne Staley's physical condition suffered immensely. Friends described him as looking like an "emaciated 80-year-old man." He had lost all his teeth, and his legs had atrophied, making walking and standing difficult. These severe health issues impacted his ability to perform, as attempts to record in early 2002 revealed his singing voice was gone and he had developed a lisp due to his lack of teeth. "In his last years, friends said he looked like an emaciated 80-year-old man. He had no teeth, his legs at atrophied, and that made walking and standing hard."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Pre-Death Decline and Drug Addiction
podcast.body: Although he officially died in April 2002, Layne Staley "might as well have been dead long before that" due to the severity of his drug addiction. This addiction prevented Alice in Chains from realizing its full potential and led their record label to give up on expectations for new material. Most of his earnings were spent on drugs. "He didn't die until April 2002, but he really might as well have been dead long before that."

xref.title: Layne Staley Found Dead April 19, 2002; William DuVall Joined, Three Albums Followed
xref.body: Layne Staley was the person around whom Alice in Chains was originally formed in 1984. By 1995, heroin had rendered him almost unable to function; the band could neither record nor tour. His body was found on April 19, 2002, in his Seattle condo after two weeks of no contact, still with a syringe in its arm. After a 2004 tsunami benefit with various substitute vocalists, the band decided to continue and eventually settled on William DuVall from a Los Angeles band called Comes with the Fall — who could blend his voice with guitarist Jerry Cantrell's harmonics and was also a capable guitarist. Three Alice in Chains albums followed. "He was also a pretty fair guitar player."

xref.body: Layne Staley died around Friday, April 5, 2002, an anniversary date shared with Kurt Cobain's death. His body was discovered on April 19, 2002, after his mother became concerned. Two days later, accountants informed his former manager, Susan Silver, that no money had been withdrawn from his bank account for two weeks. When his mother returned to the condo and heard his usually quiet cat, Sadie, meowing excessively, she called 911. Police broke in and found Staley's body with drug paraphernalia scattered nearby; an autopsy determined he had been dead for approximately two weeks. xref.body: The version of Alice in Chains featuring William DuVall has released as many full albums as the band did with Layne Staley on vocals. "This version has now released as many full albums with Duval as they had with lane."

xref.title: Formation and Name Origin
xref.body: Layne Staley had been living with a homeless Jerry Cantrell at their rehearsal space when Sleeze, Staley's band, was eventually renamed Alice in Chains. After Staley's other band (a funk outfit) and Cantrell's separate project both broke up, Cantrell and Sean Kinney asked Staley to be the vocalist for their new group, adopting the name of Staley's former band, Alice in Chains, for the new project. "Sleeze was eventually renamed Alice in Chains, while Lane was living with a homeless Jerry Cantrell at their rehearsal space."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Founding Members and Early Lineup
xref.body: Guitarist Jerry Cantrell and drummer Sean Kinney were the founders of Alice in Chains. Layne Staley was not a founder; he was drafted in early from a glam band called Sleeze, for whom he played drums. "That was guitarist Jerry Cantrell and drummer Sean Kinney. But he was drafted in early from another band, a glam group called Sleeze, for whom he played drums."

xref.title: Friendships with Notable Musicians and Figures
xref.body: Mark Lanegan was close friends with Chef Anthony Bourdain, for whom he wrote an obituary, as well as Layne Staley of Alice in Chains, Eddie Vedder, the members of Soundgarden, and Kurt Cobain. "He was also good friends with Chef Anthony Bourdain. He wrote an obituary on Bourdain when he died. He was also buddies with doomed Ellison Chainsinger, Lane Staley. Other friends included Eddie Vedder, all the guys in Soundgarden and Kurt Cobain."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Layne Staley's Continued Tenure Despite Drug Use
xref.body: The band retained Layne Staley despite his drug problems, keeping him "until he drugged himself to death," highlighting a perceived double standard in how the band handled substance abuse among its members. "yet they kept senior Lane Staley until he drugged himself to death."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Layne Staley's Decline and Isolation
xref.body: Following his girlfriend's overdose death in 1996, Layne Staley's drug hell intensified, and he largely withdrew from the world, living a hermetic existence in a condo. During this period, he spent his time painting, playing video games, and doing drugs, while his physical health rapidly deteriorated. His arms became covered with sores that threatened to become gangrenous, his teeth rotted, and his weight plummeted to around one hundred pounds, as he could only keep down protein drinks. "He lived a hermetic existence in a condo, painting and playing video games and doing drugs."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Layne Staley's Decline and Isolation (Late Original Existence)
xref.body: In the band's final years of original existence, singer Layne Staley became a "super hard core junkie," largely confined to his condo, painting, playing video games, and injecting smack. He rarely ventured out, had drugs delivered, and lost teeth due to malnutrition. "And this is because senior Lane Staley had turned into such a super hard court junkie, and he wasn't able to do much of anything except staying his condo and paint and play video games and shoot smack into his veins."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 1

xref.title: Layne Staley's Drug Addiction and Decline
xref.body: Around 1995, Layne Staley's drug habit spiraled out of control, leading to his virtual disappearance from 1996 onward. His last performance with the band was on July 3, 1996, in Kansas City, during a tour with KISS. He became a severe addict, barricading himself in his Seattle condo, where he painted, played video games, and had drugs delivered, leaving the band paralyzed. "Lane turned into an irreparable junkie, barricading himself in his Seattle condo where he painted, played video games, and had all his drugs delivered to the door."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Layne Staley's Heroin Addiction
xref.body: Layne Staley, singer for Alice in Chains, began using heroin in the early 1990s. Despite numerous attempts at rehabilitation, he was unable to maintain sobriety. The death of Kurt Cobain in 1994 initially scared him, but he soon returned to his drug use. After his girlfriend died of an overdose in 1996, Staley's addiction worsened, leading him to lose the will to live, become hermetic, and render him unable to tour or record with Alice in Chains. "He started shooting heroin in the early 1990s, and despite several attempts at rehab, nothing stuck."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Layne Staley's Inherited Addiction
xref.body: Layne Staley's father was a heavy drug user, suggesting a family history of addiction. "Lane's father was a heavy drug user, so like father, like son."

xref.title: Layne Staley's Pre-Alice in Chains Band
xref.body: Sleeze was a glam group where Layne Staley played drums before he was drafted into the band that would eventually become Alice in Chains. Sleeze was later renamed Alice in Chains. "He was drafted in early from another band, a glam group called Sleeze, for whom he played drums."

xref.title: Layne Staley's Vocal Style
xref.body: Layne Staley's voice and his harmonies with Jerry Cantrell were central to the band's sound, considered the best hard rock harmonies since David Lee Roth and Michael Anthony in Van Halen's early days. Their vocal arrangements often featured dual lead vocals, strategically overlapped, with the two voices typically separated by a major third. Staley, with the more powerful delivery, could transition from a menacing monotone to sharp, cutting explosions, and also had a great scream, appealing to both metal and alternative fans. "Technically, the two voices were separated by a major third with Lane having the more powerful of the two deliveries."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Loss of Members
xref.body: The band experienced tragic losses, with John Baker Saunders dying of a heroin overdose on January 15, 1999, and Layne Staley later dying from drug-related causes. "John Baker Saunders died of a hair run overdose on January 15, 1999."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Mariah O'Brien's Cover Shoot
xref.body: Mariah O'Brien, known for appearing on Spinal Tap's "Bitch School" single, posed for the *Dirt* album cover on June 14, 1992. She lay in the body-shaped hole in the studio's "desert" set for eight hours while photographer Rocky Schenk took hundreds of shots and adjusted lighting. O'Brien later recalled having to hold her urge to urinate during the lengthy session. It was clarified that O'Brien, not singer Layne Staley's then-girlfriend Demri Parrott, is the woman on the cover. Today, Mariah O'Brien works as an interior designer in Los Angeles. "Mariah had to lie in that hole for eight hours as Schenk took hundreds of shots, adjusting the lighting countless times."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Stories Behind Iconic Album Covers Part 1

xref.title: Participation in Mad Season Project
xref.body: Despite his severe addiction, Layne Staley managed to participate in the Mad Season project. Mike McCready and John Baker Saunders supported him through the recording sessions, hoping that working with sober musicians might offer him a moment of clarity, but it ultimately did not help him achieve lasting sobriety. "Mike McCready and John Baker Saunders pulled Lane through those sessions, hoping that being around sober musicians would produce a moment of clarity, but it didn't."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Regular Checks on Layne Staley (Years Leading to Death)
xref.body: Alice in Chains drummer Sean Kinney made a concerted effort to check on Layne Staley during his years of isolation and decline. Kinney would check in at Staley's condo at least three times a week, demonstrating a commitment to ensuring his bandmate was "okay, or as okay as circumstances allowed." However, Staley was often unresponsive to calls or knocks at his door. "Meanwhile, Allison Chains drummer Sean Kinney made sure that he checked in online at his condo at least three times a week, just to make sure that everything was okay, or as okay as circumstances allowed."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Rehab Attempts and Band Support
xref.body: Layne Staley made several attempts at rehab, often in Los Angeles facilities, achieving brief periods of sobriety. At one point, all members of Alice in Chains flew to Los Angeles weekly to participate in his sessions, showing their support. "He enrolled in rehab several times, usually at a facility in Los Angeles, and each time he got sober for a bit."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Temporary Sobriety after Kurt Cobain's Death
xref.body: Layne Staley was temporarily "scared straight" by the death of Kurt Cobain, but he resumed drug use within weeks. "Lane was briefly scared straight by the death of Kurt Cobain, but within weeks he was back at it."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Time Apart (4 years, 9 months, 18 days)
xref.body: The band was effectively apart for this duration, measured from Layne Staley's death (April 19, 2002) to their first performance with new singer William DuVall (September 22, 2006). "So that's a break of four years, nine months, and 18 days."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 1

xref.title: Unreached Potential Due to Drug Use
xref.body: Alice in Chains was considered a "great band" with a "different and intriguing" sound and image. However, there is a "lingering feeling that they never reached their full potential" primarily because Layne Staley, and frankly the rest of the band, were heavily preoccupied with drug use. "Alison Chains, make no mistake about it, was a great band."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: William DuVall Joins as Lead Vocalist
xref.body: Following a successful show in March 2006, where William DuVall (singer for Comes with the Fall) performed as a guest vocalist, the band considered him for a permanent role. They had known and respected DuVall for five or six years. Other candidates, like Vinny Dombrowski of Sponge, were considered but didn't fit, and Scott Weiland was deemed unsuitable due to his drug issues. DuVall was chosen because he sounded close to Layne Staley without being a clone. His integration was gradual, leading to a full commitment by late 2008. "One of the guest vocalists that evening was a guy named William Duval, the singer with a group called Comes with the Fall."
